questions.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator and how do you secure its endpoints in production?
questions.title: Spring Boot Actuator — Endpoints and Security
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot Actuator exposes operational HTTP (and JMX) endpoints for health checks, metrics, info, environment, thread dumps, and more. By default only /health and /info are exposed over HTTP; all others must be explicitly enabled. In production you should restrict actuator endpoints to an internal management port or secure them with Spring Security role-based access control to prevent information disclosure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows that Actuator endpoints are a security risk if left open and can describe a layered defence strategy.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Exposing management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* in production without any authentication, leaking environment variables, heap dumps, and internal metrics.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe using a separate management.server.port with a firewall rule so only internal services reach Actuator, plus /actuator/health groups for liveness and readiness probes in Kubernetes.

sections.title: Actuator Is Production Observability Out of the Box — And a Security Liability If Left Open
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator adds production-ready endpoints to your application — `/health`, `/metrics`, `/env`, `/beans`, `/heapdump`, `/threaddump`, and more. These endpoints give you instant visibility into your running application without writing any custom monitoring code. The problem is that several of these endpoints expose **dangerously sensitive information.**

`/env` shows every environment variable — including database passwords and API keys if they're injected that way. `/heapdump` lets anyone download a full heap snapshot containing in-memory secrets, session tokens, and decrypted credentials. `/beans` reveals your entire application architecture. Setting `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*` in production — which many tutorials recommend for development — is the most common Actuator security mistake.

**The default in Spring Boot 2.x+ is conservative by design:** only `/health` and `/info` are exposed over HTTP. Everything else requires explicit opt-in. But the real production strategy isn't just about which endpoints to expose — it's a layered defense combining endpoint selection, authentication, network isolation, and health check design.

sections.title: Controlling Exposure — Which Endpoints to Enable and How to Lock Down the Rest
Network Isolation — The Separate Management Port That Changes Everything
sections.content:
The strongest security measure isn't authentication — it's **network isolation.** Setting `management.server.port=9090` moves all Actuator endpoints to a separate port. In Kubernetes or any cloud deployment, you expose port 8080 to the internet through the ingress but keep port 9090 accessible only from the internal network.

This means `/heapdump`, `/env`, and `/threaddump` are never reachable from the public internet regardless of authentication configuration. Even if someone discovers a vulnerability in your security setup, the management port isn't routed through the load balancer. Combine this with `management.server.address=127.0.0.1` in single-server deployments to bind management endpoints exclusively to localhost.

The management port also supports its own SSL configuration via `management.server.ssl.*` properties, so you can require mutual TLS for internal services accessing Actuator while serving the main app over standard HTTPS.

sections.title: Health Groups — Separate Liveness and Readiness Probes for Kubernetes
sections.content:
Spring Boot 2.3+ introduced **health groups** that solve a specific Kubernetes problem: liveness and readiness probes need different health indicators. A liveness probe should check "is this process alive and not deadlocked" — if it fails, Kubernetes restarts the pod. A readiness probe should check "can this pod serve traffic" — if it fails, the pod is removed from the service's endpoints.

Including a database health check in the liveness probe is a common mistake. If the database goes down, every pod gets restarted — which is worse than useless because the database is still down and now you've triggered a cascading restart. The database check belongs in the readiness probe, where a failure means "stop sending traffic to this pod" but doesn't trigger a restart.

Spring Boot exposes `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness` automatically when running in a Kubernetes environment (detected via the `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` environment variable). You configure which indicators belong to each group in properties. The readiness group typically includes database, Redis, and message broker checks, while liveness stays minimal — usually just the default ping.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Never expose `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*` in production** — `/actuator/env` dumps all properties including passwords and tokens; `/actuator/heapdump` gives attackers the full JVM heap.
- **Separate management port isolates actuator from the application** — `management.server.port=9090` with a firewall rule that blocks port 9090 from public internet is the production-safe pattern.
- **`/actuator/health` vs `/actuator/health/**` have different content** — the root endpoint shows `UP`/`DOWN`; the detail endpoints (`/actuator/health/db`, `/actuator/health/diskSpace`) show component-level information that may leak connection strings.
- **Custom `HealthIndicator` beans integrate external checks** — implement `HealthIndicator`, return `Health.up()` or `Health.down().withDetail("reason", msg)`; Spring Boot includes it in `/health` automatically.
- **`/actuator/metrics` and `/actuator/prometheus` expose performance data** — integrate with Prometheus/Grafana by adding `micrometer-registry-prometheus`; no code changes required beyond the dependency.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator gives you production visibility — health checks, metrics, environment inspection, thread dumps — without deploying a separate monitoring agent. The default configuration is safe for development. Exposing it fully in production is a security incident waiting to happen.

**Security hardening**
- By default only `/health` and `/info` are exposed over HTTP
- `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*` exposes everything — including `/env` (dumps all properties with passwords), `/heapdump` (full JVM memory), `/shutdown` (remote shutdown)
- Expose only what monitoring infrastructure needs: `include=health,info,metrics,prometheus`

**Isolating the management port**
- `management.server.port=9090` moves all actuator endpoints to a separate port
- A firewall or network policy allows only internal monitoring systems to reach port 9090; port 8080 remains public-facing
- This is the standard pattern for production: no authentication overhead on the main port, no public exposure on the management port

**Health endpoint detail**
- `/actuator/health` returns only `UP` or `DOWN` by default — safe to expose publicly for load balancer checks
- `management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized` reveals database connection status and disk space only to authenticated users

Custom `HealthIndicator` beans are how you add application-specific checks — external API reachability, queue depth thresholds, license expiry — integrated into the same `/health` response that your monitoring system already watches.

steps: The first layer of defense is exposure control.
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include accepts a comma-separated list of endpoint IDs.
For production, expose only what you need — typically health, metrics, info, and prometheus (if you use Prometheus for monitoring).
The next layer is Spring Security.
With spring-boot-starter-security on the classpath, you can restrict Actuator endpoints by role.
A typical configuration secures all management endpoints behind an ACTUATOR role while leaving /health and /info public for load balancer checks.
